answer: LINE (Tang et al., 2015) does not require supervised data to learn its embeddings. It is an unsupervised method that preserves first-order and second-order proximity through edge sampling and optimizes an objective over the network structure alone. Labels are needed only when the embeddings are evaluated downstream, for example by training a classifier (such as logistic regression) on node vectors to predict labels, or by adding a supervised term if one chooses a semi-supervised variant. DeepWalk (Perozzi et al., 2014) is likewise unsupervised in its representation learning: it runs random walks and applies skip-gram. On BlogCatalog, DeepWalk is evaluated with the same downstream protocol. Labels are used only in a multi-label node classification task, in which a one-vs-rest logistic regression is trained on a varying fraction of labeled nodes (e.g., 10%–90%), with Micro-F1 and Macro-F1 averaged over random splits. The contrast is therefore less about how each method learns and more about where labels enter. Both learn label-free embeddings and use labels only for evaluation. The difference is that DeepWalk's original paper reports BlogCatalog results, whereas LINE's original paper, to my recollection, used other datasets such as Flickr, YouTube, Orkut, and Twitter, so any BlogCatalog comparison for LINE comes from later papers.
confidence_reasoning: The core claim that both methods are unsupervised with labels used only for downstream evaluation is well established, but the details of the BlogCatalog evaluation protocol and which datasets LINE's original paper used are less certain from memory.
